findings.headline: PWLB rates rose sharply in March 2026 as gilt market sold off on geopolitical risk
findings.detail: 1-year PWLB borrowing rates jumped 67 basis points from 4.37% in January to 5.04% in March 2026. The 10-year rate rose from 5.38% to 5.72% and 25-year from 6.01% to 6.29%. This follows gilt yield moves described as material reversals of earlier-year falls, driven by Middle East conflict and ongoing Ukraine tensions.
findings.matters: Rate environment directly impacts refinance costs; £50m position coming due in 2026/27 will face these elevated rates
findings.figures: 1-year PWLB: 5.04% (March 2026); 10-year: 5.72%; 25-year: 6.29%; market base rate 3.75% throughout period from December 2025 onwards
findings.quote: Borrowing became increasingly expensive during 2025/26 and into early 2026/27. Gilt yields rose materially in March 2026, more than reversing the falls earlier in the financial year.

findings.headline: Short-term borrowing from 2024/25 must be refinanced in 2026/27 at substantially higher rates
findings.detail: The council faced cash pressures in 2024/25 from overspending and heavy capital spending, forcing it to borrow short-term on the local authority market. In February-March 2025 it refinanced with a £50m PWLB loan at rates that have since risen sharply. This short-term position must now be rolled at higher rates due to Middle East conflict and gilt market moves, resulting in materially higher debt servicing costs in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Rising refinance costs reduce budget flexibility and increase vulnerability to further rate movements; overspending-driven borrowing is a structural concern, not temporary
findings.figures: £50m PWLB refinancing; 1-year PWLB rates: 4.37% (January 2026) to 5.04% (March 2026); 10-year: 5.38% to 5.72%
findings.quote: In 2024/25, the Council's cash levels were impacted by the overspending position, and the large value of capital costs being paid in year. This resulted in the Council borrowing short-term on the local authority market, before borrowing £50m from the Public Works Loans Board when rates fell in February and March 2025. This short-term borrowing has had to be replaced in early 2026/27 after rates had risen due to the conflict in the Middle East, and will be reflected in higher borrowing costs in 2026/27.

findings.headline: PFI restatement increased liabilities by £50.8m and breached operational borrowing limits
findings.detail: IFRS16 accounting changes required restatement of two PFI scheme liabilities in 2024/25: Mersey Gateway Bridge +£46.1m and The Grange School +£4.7m, calculated using indexed rather than original unitary charges. This caused the council to breach its Operational Boundary at 31 March 2025, which was only corrected retrospectively in March 2026.
findings.matters: Operational boundary breaches signal forecasting or governance failure, and PFI liabilities constrain a council's future borrowing capacity and cash flexibility
findings.figures: £46.1m (Mersey Gateway), £4.7m (Grange School); Operational Boundary moved from £558.3m actual 2024/25 to £644.5m actual 2025/26
findings.quote: The Council hold two PFI Schemes, for The Grange School, whose liability was increased by £4.7m and for the Mersey Gateway Bridge, whose liability increased by £46.1m during 2024/25. These values were updated after the approval of the 2025/26 Treasury Management Strategy Statement, leading to a breach in the Operational Boundary at the end of the 2024/25 financial year.

findings.headline: Continued pressures within the SEND system identified as a governance issue
findings.detail: The council explicitly lists 'Continued pressures within the SEND system' as one of five significant governance issues for 2025/26. SEND (Special Educational Needs and Disabilities) is a known budget pressure area across councils, often resulting in overspending and deficit funding arrangements.
findings.matters: SEND pressures are a material budget risk for councils and, when flagged as a governance issue requiring sustained attention, suggest the council has not yet stabilised this area. This directly affects financial forecasts and borrowing needs.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Continued pressures within the SEND system

findings.headline: Identified weakness in integrating risk, performance and financial management
findings.detail: The council has flagged 'the need to strengthen integration of risk, performance and financial management' as a significant governance issue. This suggests gaps exist in how the council connects its financial decision-making to risk assessment and performance tracking—a key control area lenders assess.
findings.matters: Weak integration of financial and risk management points to potential gaps in identifying emerging financial problems early, a material concern for lenders assessing the council's financial control environment.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: The need to strengthen integration of risk, performance and financial management

findings.headline: Financial sustainability identified as a significant governance challenge requiring sustained management focus
findings.detail: The Annual Governance Statement explicitly lists 'Financial sustainability and the delivery of transformation' as one of five significant governance issues for 2025/26. The council acknowledges these issues 'will require sustained management focus' and are 'consistent with the Council's wider risk environment'. No specific deficit or savings shortfall is quantified, but the formal identification in the governance statement indicates this is an active concern at board level.
findings.matters: A lender evaluating this council needs to understand that financial sustainability is flagged as a governance issue requiring ongoing attention, not routine pressure. It signals the council itself has identified concerns about its financial trajectory or transformation delivery.
findings.figures: None provided in the statement
findings.quote: Financial sustainability and the delivery of transformation [are among] a number of significant governance issues for 2025/26. These issues are consistent with the Council's wider risk environment and will require sustained management focus.

findings.paper_title: AG Board 240626 - External Auditors Annual Report 2425 - Action Plan Progress Update v3
findings.headline: Financial plans include provision to replenish council reserves in future years.
findings.detail: The MTFS includes plans to replenish reserves in future years, indicating that reserves have been drawn down to support the current budget position.
findings.matters: Using reserves to balance budgets is not sustainable. The council's plans to replenish reserves show it recognises this, but highlights past reliance on reserves to manage budget pressures.
findings.figures: None specific; reserves to be replenished from underspends and savings
findings.quote: It also includes plans to replenish Council reserves in future years.

findings.paper_title: AG Board 240626 - External Auditors Annual Report 2425 - Action Plan Progress Update v3
findings.headline: MTFS extended to five years (2026-2030) to reflect the council's challenging financial circumstances and financial risks.
findings.detail: The Medium Term Financial Strategy has been extended from the normal planning period to five years, an unusual step taken because of the council's challenging financial circumstances and financial risks.
findings.matters: Extending planning horizons signals the council expects financial pressure to persist for several years rather than being a short-term issue.
findings.figures: MTFS covers 2026-2030 (five years)
findings.quote: The MTFS has been extended to cover five years from 2026/27, to reflect the Council's challenging financial circumstances and financial risks.

findings.paper_title: AG Board 240626 - External Auditors Annual Report 2425 - Action Plan Progress Update v3
findings.headline: Independent Improvement Board with five independent experts established and meeting monthly for at least six months, supported by LGA and MHCLG.
findings.detail: Due to the seriousness of the council's financial position, an independently chaired Improvement Board including five independent experts has been established with support from central government. The board meets monthly to scrutinise the improvement work.
findings.matters: The establishment of an independent board with government support indicates serious external concerns about the council's governance and financial sustainability. This level of intervention is rare and signals distress.
findings.figures: Five independent experts; monthly meetings for at least six months
findings.quote: In order to strengthen the governance of the improvement journey, the Council with support from the Local Government Association (LGA) and the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG), has established an Improvement Board which is independently chaired and includes five independent experts. The Board is meeting monthly for at least six months, to support and scrutinise progress with the improvement work.

findings.paper_title: AG Board 240626 - External Auditors Annual Report 2425 - Action Plan Progress Update v3
findings.headline: Significant additional financial provision made for demand-led services including children's residential placements, fostering, transport and adult care due to experiencing significant financial pressures.
findings.detail: The MTFS includes significant additional financial provision for children's residential placements, independent fostering, home-to-school transport, adults community care, direct payments and in-house care homes, all flagged as experiencing significant pressures.
findings.matters: These are statutory or demand-driven services where cost increases are not wholly within the council's control. This suggests underlying demand or cost-per-case inflation the council cannot manage down.
findings.figures: None specified by amount, but described as significant additional provision
findings.quote: Similar details and significant additional financial provision have been included within the Strategy for the key demand-led services experiencing significant financial pressures including; children's residential placements, independent fostering, home to school transport, adults community care, direct payments and in-house care homes.

findings.paper_title: AG Board 240626 - External Auditors Annual Report 2425 - Action Plan Progress Update v3
findings.headline: Government will fund 90% (£25m) of accumulated SEND deficit as at 31 March 2026, but future-years' funding remains uncertain until statutory override expires 31 March 2028.
findings.detail: The DfE has approved the council's SEND Reform Plan and committed to High Needs Stability Grant funding covering 90% of the accumulated deficit (£25m). However, government has not committed to similar funding for deficits accruing in 2026/27 and 2027/28, creating uncertainty.
findings.matters: SEND is a statutory service with demand-driven costs. While the £25m is funded, the council could face further significant deficits if future-year funding is not forthcoming, potentially requiring more EFS borrowing.
findings.figures: £25m (90% of accumulated SEND deficit as at 31 March 2026); deficit issue runs until 31 March 2028
findings.quote: Government has recognised that a national solution is required. As part of the 2026/27 final grant settlement the Government confirmed that High Needs Stability Grant funding would be provided to fund 90% (£25m) of the accumulated deficit as at 31 March 2026.

findings.paper_title: AG Board 240626 - External Auditors Annual Report 2425 - Action Plan Progress Update v3
findings.headline: Agency staffing in Children's social care reduced from 63% to 18%, though agency costs remain a significant budget pressure requiring continued comprehensive plans.
findings.detail: Children's services have successfully reduced agency staffing from 63% to 18% (below national average), but agency costs are highlighted as a significant ongoing cost pressure across the council. Work continues corporately and in service directorates to address these pressures.
findings.matters: High agency staffing indicates service delivery problems and is significantly more expensive than permanent staff. The large previous level suggests service delivery challenges; ongoing pressure suggests the problem persists in other areas.
findings.figures: Children's social care agency staffing: 63% to 18% reduction
findings.quote: It outlines the particular pressure of agency staff costs and the work being undertaken corporately and across service directorates to address these pressures. As a result Children's social care is now operating with 18% agency staffing, which is less than the national average, compared to 63% a year ago.

findings.paper_title: AG Board 240626 - External Auditors Annual Report 2425 - Action Plan Progress Update v3
findings.headline: Council faces significant structural budget deficit requiring £35.5m savings over four years.
findings.detail: The council has set savings targets totalling £35.5m across the three years following 2026/27, based on benchmarking against comparator councils. This reflects the scale of the structural imbalance between the council's income and its spending.
findings.matters: A structural deficit of this scale indicates the council cannot deliver balanced budgets without major service transformation. The council's ability to deliver these savings on schedule is critical to its financial recovery.
findings.figures: £35.5m savings targets set across four-year period (2026/27 and following three years)
findings.quote: The savings proposals were developed into an Improvement Plan, with detailed savings identified for 2026/27 and targets set for each Directorate for the following three years totalling £35.5m.

findings.paper_title: AG Board 240626 - External Auditors Annual Report 2425 - Action Plan Progress Update v3
findings.headline: Council required £14.7m Exceptional Financial Support borrowing in 2025/26, down from £29m forecast.
findings.detail: The council needed government-supported borrowing to balance its budget. While a £14.6m underspend halved the requirement from forecast, EFS remains essential to the council's finances, indicating it cannot balance its budget without government support.
findings.matters: EFS is a signal of financial distress and means the council's finances are dependent on annual government support decisions. Lenders use this as a key indicator of creditworthiness.
findings.figures: £14.7m EFS borrowing 2025/26; £29m forecast; £14.6m underspend
findings.quote: As a result the outturn position for the year shows a significant underspend of £14.6m against budget, enabling the Council to half the amount of EFS borrowing required for the year from £29m to £14.7m.

findings.headline: Capital programme delivery at 81.4% suggests implementation delays; £23.555m of planned spending did not occur
findings.detail: Capital spending reached £43.953m of planned £54.006m (81.4% delivery, assuming 20% planned slippage). This means £23.555m of originally planned capital spending either did not occur or was re-phased. Notable slippage in Children's SEND (£1.775m unallocated), Environment & Regeneration Pride in Place (£0.75m remaining), East Runcorn Connectivity (£6.085m remaining), and multiple other schemes. Large new schemes like Sci-tech Daresbury Project Violet (£2.2m) and Sci-tech Daresbury CPO (£3.0m) show £0 spending in 2025/26.
findings.matters: Capital slippage can indicate delivery capacity constraints, funding challenges, or scheme reprioritization. When a council struggles to spend its planned capital programme, particularly on strategic regeneration, it signals either that the programme is unrealistic or that the council lacks capacity to deliver. This matters to lenders assessing the council's ability to realize economic benefits from investment.
findings.figures: Capital spending £43.953m of £54.006m planned = 81.4% delivery; £23.555m did not spend as planned
findings.quote: Capital spending at 31st March 2026 totalled £43.953m, which is 81.4% of the planned spending of £54.006m (which assumes a 20% slippage between years)

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £14.469m continues to accumulate, with High Needs spend at £43.096m against allocation of £29.760m (£13.336m gap)
findings.detail: The DSG deficit carries forward on the balance sheet due to a statutory override, currently set to end 31 March 2028. However, government recently confirmed it will fund up to 90% of High Needs deficits from 1 April 2028 and responsibility will shift to Central Government—but this is dependent on councils implementing SEND Reform Plans. Meanwhile, high needs spending in 2025/26 is £43.096m against allocation of £29.760m, a gap of £13.336m. This gap widened: the council anticipated a £9.4m shortfall at budget-setting but it increased by £3.936m during the year. The interest cost to the General Fund for managing the DSG deficit is £0.891m annually.
findings.matters: Although government may take on responsibility for DSG deficits from 2028, there are conditions (SEND Reform Plans) and until then the council bears the cost and risk. The widening gap (£3.936m deterioration in-year) suggests SEND cost pressures are accelerating. If government does not fully fund as promised, or if the council cannot implement acceptable reform plans, the deficit could again become a council liability after 2028.
findings.figures: DSG deficit £14.469m; High Needs spend £43.096m vs allocation £29.760m = £13.336m gap; gap widened by £3.936m in-year; interest cost £0.891m
findings.quote: Full year expenditure for all demands on High Needs funding are £43.096m, which is a substantial amount in excess of the present High Needs allocation of £29.760m, a difference of £13.336m

findings.headline: Outstanding sundry debt increased £2.287m (13.8%) to £18.860m, with Adult Social Care debt up £1.389m to £14.705m
findings.detail: Aged outstanding debt rose significantly: total overdue debt now £18.860m vs £16.573m prior year, an increase of £2.287m or 13.8%. Adult Social Care accounts for £14.705m of this (78% of total), up £1.389m. The council notes that higher debt levels represent 'missed opportunities' for investment income, estimating £45k foregone per £1m of outstanding debt annually. The report acknowledges 'additional work is undertaken to analyse the debt in more detail to enable more prompt recovery action.'
findings.matters: Rising debt levels indicate increasing service users unable or unwilling to pay for adult social care. This is both a cash flow problem (delaying receipt of revenue) and a collection risk problem (debt may not be recoverable). The concentration in Adult Social Care suggests the problem is with individuals receiving care, not institutional non-payers, making recovery challenging.
findings.figures: Total outstanding debt £18.860m (up £2.287m/13.8%); Adult Social Care £14.705m (up £1.389m); estimated £45k foregone income per £1m debt
findings.quote: The greatest concern in terms of outstanding debt is with the Adult Social Care Directorate, there has been an increase in debt, as at 31 March 2026 the amount outstanding was £14.705m, an increase of £1.389m over the year

findings.headline: General Reserve at £5.147m represents only 2.81% of net budget and is described as 'minimum level' providing 'little provision for unforeseen or exceptional costs'
findings.detail: The council's General Reserve is unchanged from the previous year at £5.147m but represents only 2.81% of the 2025/26 net budget of £183.052m. The finance director explicitly states this 'is considered to be the minimum level and provides little provision for unforeseen or exceptional costs going forward.' The council aspires to replenish this at £2m per year 'where affordable' but given ongoing EFS dependency this is unlikely.
findings.matters: A 2.81% reserve is extremely low and offers no buffer for in-year pressures or emergencies. Authorities typically maintain reserves of 5-10% of budget. This council is operating with minimal contingency and has no financial flexibility to absorb even modest adverse variances.
findings.figures: General Reserve £5.147m = 2.81% of £183.052m net budget; target replenishment £2m per year
findings.quote: This level of General Reserve is considered to be the minimum level and provides little provision for unforeseen or exceptional costs going forward

findings.headline: School Transport out-of-borough overspend of £0.424m driven by increasing SEN pupil numbers and unachieved £0.3m efficiency savings
findings.detail: The council has 653 pupils on school transport, 161 attending out-of-borough schools. Out-of-borough transport overspent by £0.424m at average cost of £10,208 per pupil vs £3,842 in-borough. This is partly offset by a £0.712m budget increase added in 2025/26 for growth. Additionally, a £0.3m efficiency saving for 'Home to School and College Travel and Transport Policy' for SEN pupils was not achieved; the consultation completed but 'any efficiencies will not be realised until Autumn 2026.'
findings.matters: This is a demand-driven cost with limited elasticity. The council has statutory responsibility to transport SEN pupils. If numbers continue rising and per-pupil costs remain high (£10k out-of-borough), this creates an uncontrollable budget pressure. The delay in implementing transport policy means this pressure will extend into 2026/27.
findings.figures: 653 total pupils; 161 out-of-borough at £10,208 per pupil; £0.424m overspend; £0.3m unachieved savings delayed to Autumn 2026
findings.quote: The Council has a statutory responsibility to provide Special Educational Needs (SEN) pupils with transport...The Out of Borough overspend has decreased compared to the previous year's overspend of £0.799m due to £0.712m added to the budget in 2025/26 for growth

findings.headline: Multiple Children's Services savings targets of £1.9m are not being achieved due to rising cost and demand pressures
findings.detail: Appendix 6 shows Children's and Families savings proposals totalling £1.9m for 2025/26, with minimal achievement: Residential Placements (£1.5m target) 'unlikely to be achieved', Fostering (£200k target) not achieved due to 'national shortage of foster carers', Legal/Court Costs (£200k target) only partially progressed. The underlying issue is that demand for children in care continues rising and unit costs are not controllable. The report documents that while some residential cost reductions were 'achieved against residential care, costs continue to remain high in comparison with benchmarked authorities.'
findings.matters: Unachieved savings are a leading indicator of structural financial instability. When a council's own projections show savings will not materialise, those are hard constraints, not conservative estimates. Children's services is one of the largest council budgets and if cost growth cannot be arrested, the entire budget trajectory is at risk.
findings.figures: £1.9m of agreed savings for 2025/26 in Children & Families; £1.5m residential, £200k fostering, £200k court costs all not achieved or unlikely to be achieved
findings.quote: Residential placements were all reviewed in early 2024 with some reduction in costs established...Whilst this saving has been achieved against residential care, costs continue to remain high in comparison with benchmarked authorities

findings.headline: Adult Social Care additional payments to providers surged 65% in a single year from £0.424m to £0.701m
findings.detail: Additional payments (where care homes charge above the contracted bed rate) increased dramatically year-on-year. The paper documents this graphically and states 'for 25/26, numbers and costs are still increasing and the spend at the end of the financial year totalled £0.701m. The cost in 2024/25 was £0.424m, therefore an increase of £0.277m (65%).' Simultaneously, domiciliary care costs per package rose 17.95% (£450.64 to £531.55) while residential care additional payments continue accumulating.
findings.matters: This is a cost-inflation problem, not demand problem. The council is locked into rising payment obligations with limited control. Lenders need to understand this trajectory: if additional payments are growing 65% annually, the council's social care budget will rapidly become unmanageable. This is ahead of any national care reform or policy change.
findings.figures: Additional payments: £0.424m (2024/25) to £0.701m (2025/26), increase of £0.277m (65%); domiciliary care cost per package up 17.95% to £531.55
findings.quote: The spend at the end of the financial year totalled £0.701m. The cost in 2024/25 was £0.424m, therefore an increase of £0.277m (65%)

findings.headline: Council still requires £14.7m of Exceptional Financial Support in 2025/26 and expects 'future EFS borrowings are expected over the medium term'
findings.detail: Despite underspending by £8.2m, the council needed to borrow £14.7m through Exceptional Financial Support to balance its 2025/26 budget (reduced from the originally approved £29.385m). The Director of Finance states 'future EFS borrowings are expected over the medium term until the Council is in a position to contain net spend within the approved budget.' This is now £24.7m of cumulative EFS across two years (£10m in 2024/25 plus £14.7m in 2025/26), with repayment costs of £3.315m budgeted for 2026/27.
findings.matters: Dependency on exceptional financial support signals structural insolvency. The council cannot balance its budget from its normal revenue sources and expects this to continue. Each year of EFS borrowing adds to repayment obligations, further squeezing future budgets.
findings.figures: £14.7m EFS requirement 2025/26; £10m EFS used 2024/25; £3.315m repayment costs 2026/27; total now £24.7m cumulative
findings.quote: Future EFS borrowings are expected over the medium term until the Council is in a position to contain net spend within the approved budget

findings.headline: £6.4m of the £8.2m underspend is one-off, non-recurring savings that will not repeat in future years
findings.detail: The council achieved a £8.242m underspend but explicitly states 'within the outturn position there are a number of one-off savings (calculated at £6.4m) which have contributed towards the position which will likely not be repeated in future years.' These include £1.3m ASC Pooled Budget contribution, £1.2m DFG capitalisation, £1.2m various grants repurposing, £1.5m unused Children's Improvement Grant, and £1.2m Business Rate Pool surplus. This reveals a structural deficit being masked.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand the underlying budget position. A council showing a balanced outturn but dependent on one-off items and continued EFS support remains at financial risk. This pattern suggests the council cannot live within its base budget.
findings.figures: £8.242m underspend, of which £6.4m is one-off; EFS requirement reduced from £29.385m to £14.7m
findings.quote: within the outturn position there are a number of one-off savings (calculated at £6.4m) which have contributed towards the position which will likely not be repeated in future years

findings.paper_title: Exec Board -090726 Capital Programme 2026.27 to 2028.29 Final
findings.headline: No capital receipts available for new capital schemes; all growth must be externally funded
findings.detail: The Council has adopted a cautious approach to capital receipts and has now exhausted discretionary capacity. Projected capital receipts balances of £2.4–2.8m over 2026/27 to 2028/29 are all committed to existing programmes. Any new capital initiatives must be funded through external grants or additional borrowing.
findings.matters: Exhausted capital receipts remove a buffer for unforeseen capital needs and force reliance on external funding or new borrowing for any programme expansion, reducing financial flexibility and dependency on external grant income.
findings.quote: The cautious approach the Council has adopted over the past number of years needs to be continued and as such there are no funds available for new capital starts unless external funding is generated to finance the cost.

findings.paper_title: Exec Board -090726 Capital Programme 2026.27 to 2028.29 Final
findings.headline: Capital programme heavily dependent on new prudential borrowing creating £1.15m annual revenue cost
findings.detail: 23% of total capital expenditure (£34.5m of £150.4m) will be funded by prudential borrowing. This creates increased revenue costs of £1.150m per year for 2026/27, 2027/28 and 2028/29, totalling £3.45m over the period, to cover principal repayment and interest. The Council must demonstrate these borrowings are affordable and sustainable under the Prudential Code.
findings.matters: Material reliance on new borrowing creates recurring revenue budget pressure; this £3.45m commitment limits financial flexibility and depends on the council's ability to service £34.5m of additional debt.
findings.figures: £34.5m borrowing (23% of total), £1.150m annual incremental revenue costs, 3-year total £3.45m
findings.quote: The capital programme is heavily funded from prudential borrowing, of total capital expenditure, £ 34.5m or 23% will come from future and existing borrowings.

findings.paper_title: Exec Board -090726 Capital Programme 2026.27 to 2028.29 Final
findings.headline: External assurance review of capital programme delivery completed in May 2026; recommendations still being addressed
findings.detail: In May 2026 the Council received a final report from Local Partnerships LLB on delivery and management of the capital programme. This review was commissioned through the LGA's Sector-led Improvement Programme funded by MHCLG. Recommendations from the review are currently being addressed by the Management Team, suggesting delivery or governance weaknesses that the Council has identified and is working to resolve.
findings.matters: An external assurance review of capital programme delivery indicates prior governance or delivery weaknesses; lenders need visibility that these are being remedied.
findings.figures: Report received 05 May 2026
findings.quote: In early 2026 the Council asked Local Partnerships LLB (via the LGA) to undertake an external assurance review, to consider the delivery and management of the Council's Capital Programme. The report included a number of recommendations which are currently being addressed by Management Team.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 26-27 - Final v2(after settlement), 12/02/2026 Executive Board
findings.headline: The council has ceased all revenue contributions to capital funding from 2027/28 onwards
findings.detail: Revenue contributions to the capital programme dropped from £205k in 2025/26 to £395k in 2026/27, then to £0 from 2027/28 onwards. This shows the council cannot spare revenue resources for capital investment and signals either exhausted revenue budgets or competing pressures requiring all revenue cash.
findings.matters: A council unable to fund even modest capital from revenue income indicates severe revenue budget strain. This pattern often precedes requests for further government support or reserve drawdowns.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 26-27 - Final v2(after settlement), 12/02/2026 Executive Board
findings.headline: Capital receipts from asset sales have collapsed to minimal levels and offer no meaningful funding flexibility
findings.detail: The council's capital receipts reserve crashed from £4.98m at the start of 2024/25 to £46k by end of 2025/26, and are budgeted to remain near-zero at £400k per year thereafter. Asset sales are declining and minimal (£1.83m planned for 2026/27), leaving the council entirely dependent on borrowing and grants for capital funding.
findings.matters: Collapsed asset sales eliminate a traditional funding valve and force reliance on borrowing or government grants. This reduces financial flexibility and increases structural dependence on external funding.
findings.figures: Capital Receipts Reserve: £4,978k (opening 2024/25), £46k (end 2025/26), £1,371k (opening 2028/29)
findings.quote: Capital Receipts - 1st April (4,978) (2,217) (46) (896) (1,371)

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 26-27 - Final v2(after settlement), 12/02/2026 Executive Board
findings.headline: The Capital Financing Requirement is growing from £669.6m to £821.6m in four years—a 23% increase in outstanding debt
findings.detail: The council's cumulative debt (measured by Capital Financing Requirement) grows from £669.6m in 2024/25 to £821.6m by 2028/29. This is driven by annual net financing needs of £55–79m, indicating relentless dependence on new borrowing to fund the capital programme. Debt service costs (MRP) are projected to more than quadruple from £3.1m to £13.4m over the same period.
findings.matters: Growing debt at this rate raises affordability concerns. Lenders must assess whether the council can service this debt from revenue and whether the trajectory is sustainable without further external support.
findings.quote: Capital Financing Requirement 669,636 694,944 730,858 769,499 821,572

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 26-27 - Final v2(after settlement), 12/02/2026 Executive Board
findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support is unexplained and growing to £74.7m by 2028/29, dominating future capital funding
findings.detail: The council's capital programme includes a line item 'Exceptional Financial Support' of £33.9m in 2026/27, growing to £74.7m by 2028/29. This is the fastest-growing and third-largest element of the capital programme, but the strategy does not explain what it is or why it is required. Without clarification, this represents an unexplained and rapidly-escalating dependency on external support.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand why a council requires exceptional government support and whether it indicates underlying financial distress or unsustainable cash pressures that could threaten loan repayment.
findings.quote: Exceptional Financial Support 10,000 30,666 33,872 56,503 74,735

findings.headline: Business rates pool (Mid-Mersey) to be dissolved; no further gains from pooling will be achieved, removing expected income.
findings.detail: Due to increased safety net protections (100% in 2026/27, reducing to 97% from 2027/28) and the new levy system on business rates growth, the risks and rewards of business rates pooling have changed unfavourably. The council has decided to dissolve the Mid-Mersey Business Rates Pool arrangement and will achieve no further gains from pooling. The council notes there is high risk that any growth achieved in 2026/27 will not be retained but will instead be used to fund safety net payments within the Liverpool City Region pilot scheme.
findings.matters: The loss of expected pooling gains removes an income source that may have been factored into medium-term planning, and the safety net ceiling limits upside from business rates growth.
findings.figures: Mid-Mersey Business Rates Pool to be dissolved; 100% safety net 2026/27, reducing to 97% 2027/28+
findings.quote: Due to the increased safety net protections, and the new levy system, there are higher risks and lower potential rewards to business rates pooling in 2026/27. As such, the Mid-Mersey Business Rates will be dissolved, and no further gains from pooling will be achieved.

findings.headline: Council tax income shortfall of £0.54m due to government's overestimated tax base growth assumption (1.23% assumed vs 0.48% actual).
findings.detail: Government's Core Spending Power calculations assumed Halton's council tax base would grow by 1.23% in 2026/27. Actual growth is forecast to reach only 0.48%, creating a £0.54m shortfall in council tax income. Because council tax income is included in the calculation of the 105% funding floor, this shortfall has a direct impact on the value of Recovery Grant Guarantee Funding received. The council notes that if actual tax base data had been used, it would have received an additional £0.54m of grant funding.
findings.matters: The government's optimistic growth assumptions have directly reduced the council's funding settlement, indicating slower economic activity or housing development than government projected.
findings.figures: Tax base growth assumed 1.23%, actual 0.48%; shortfall £0.54m
findings.quote: Government have assumed 1.23% of growth to Halton's tax base, but actual growth will only reach 0.48%, which equates to a shortfall in Council Tax income of approximately £0.54m. Due to Council Tax income being included in the calculation of the 105% funding floor, this shortfall has a direct impact on the value of Recovery Grant Guarantee Funding received.

findings.headline: Government rejected Halton's request for increased council tax flexibility; application for 7.99% rise denied, limiting revenue to 4.99%.
findings.detail: Halton applied to MHCLG on 18 December 2025 for permission to raise council tax by 7.99% in total (5.99% general increase plus 2% adult social care precept), which would have raised Band D council tax to approximately the national average level and generated anticipated additional revenue of £2.056m. On 9 February 2026, Government confirmed it would not grant any additional council tax flexibility to Halton. The council is therefore limited to 4.99% increase (2.99% general increase plus 2% adult social care precept), representing a £2.056m shortfall against the requested flexibility.
findings.matters: The rejection indicates government does not view Halton as having discretion to raise additional revenue through taxation, constraining the council's options for managing the structural deficit.
findings.figures: £2.056m anticipated from rejected 7.99% increase; council tax increase limited to 4.99%; Band D £1,938.81 (increase of £92.15 or 4.99%)
findings.quote: Halton applied to MHCLG for permission to raise council tax in 2026/27 by 7.99% in total (5.99% general council tax increase, plus 2% adult social care precept), which would have raised Band D council tax to approximately the national average level. The additional flexibility requested was anticipated to generate £2.056m. On 9th February 2026, Government confirmed that they would not grant any additional council tax flexibility to Halton for 2026/27.

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review delivered significantly less funding growth than anticipated, with Halton's 2028/29 CSP approximately £13m lower than summer 2025 projection.
findings.detail: In summer 2025, modelling suggested Halton's Core Spending Power (CSP) would increase by approximately 20% over the three-year settlement (2026/27 to 2028/29). However, changes to the Relative Needs Formulae between consultation and settlement reduced the increase to 10.22%. The final settlement improved this to 12.2%, but Halton's CSP in 2028/29 will be approximately £13m lower than anticipated in summer 2025. The primary cause was the government's greater weighting to housing costs in the updated Indices of Multiple Deprivation (IMD), which redistributed children's services funding away from northern authorities towards London. Halton's Children and Young People's Relative Needs Share reduced by 14%.
findings.matters: The £13m reduction in anticipated multi-year funding represents a material blow to financial planning. This validates the council's growing medium-term deficits and indicates government expectations for service reductions.
findings.figures: Expected CSP growth: 20% (summer 2025 modelling) → 10.22% (provisional settlement) → 12.2% (final settlement); £13m reduction in 2028/29 CSP; Children's Needs Share reduced 14%
findings.quote: Based on modelling carried out in Summer 2025, it was anticipated that Halton's Core Spending Power (CSP) would increase by approximately 20% between 2025/26 and 2028/29. Changes made between the issuing of the consultation in June 2025 and the Provisional Settlement in December 2025 had reduced this increase to 10.22%... Halton's CSP in 2028/29 will be approximately £13m lower than was anticipated in Summer 2025.

findings.headline: £5.158m of proposed 2026/27 savings includes multiple unquantified proposals marked 'TBC' (To Be Confirmed), creating delivery risk.
findings.detail: Of the £5.158m savings proposals, several material items remain unquantified and marked TBC, including: Adults with Learning Disabilities model of care (TBC), Community Care implementation (TBC), Adult Social Care staff recruitment (TBC), Prevention and Wellbeing Service review (TBC), Targeted Early Help Services review (TBC), Children in Care review (TBC), fleet rationalisation (TBC), accommodation review (TBC), and external funding review (TBC). The Finance Officer states in Section 3.21.5 that 'greater risk is identified within the planned 2026/27 savings' and 'failure to act and achieve these savings within the correct timeframe will have a detrimental impact on the Council's finances.'
findings.matters: Unquantified savings proposals indicate the savings plan is incomplete and untested. If these TBC items do not materialise at expected levels, the council will face a further deficit with no mitigating actions identified.
findings.figures: £5.158m total savings; £1.546m (supplies and services), £500k (contingency), £500k (balance sheet), £1.238m (residential care step-down) quantified; remainder TBC
findings.quote: Greater risk is also identified within the planned 2026/27 savings. Failure to act and achieve these savings within the correct timeframe will have a detrimental impact on the Council's finances.

findings.headline: General Fund reserves at minimum acceptable level with only £5.4m available for immediate need; unable to absorb in-year overspends.
findings.detail: The council holds total general and earmarked reserves of £54.9m, but only £5.4m is available for immediate need. The remaining reserves are committed for specific purposes. The Section 25 statement explicitly states the General Fund is at minimum acceptable level and unable to fund any in-year overspend in 2025/26. The council has been reliant on reserves to meet budget pressures and is now insufficient to meet current and future deficits. A plan to grow reserves by £2m per year from 2027/28 has been proposed but this is contingent on achieving savings.
findings.matters: Depleted reserves mean the council has no buffer against demand shocks, interest rate volatility, or overspends. The explicit statement that reserves cannot absorb 2025/26 overspends indicates the council is operating at the margin.
findings.figures: Total reserves £54.9m; available for immediate need £5.4m; remaining £49.5m committed
findings.quote: It is considered that the balance of the Council's General Fund is at the minimum acceptable level, and is therefore unable to fund any in-year overspend in the 2025/26 financial year... The council is now in a position where useable reserves are insufficient to meet the current and future budget deficits.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit forecast to reach £90.3m by 2029/30, with government override expiring 31 March 2028.
findings.detail: The council faces a cascading DSG deficit driven by High Needs demand and costs. The cumulative deficit is forecast at £27.2m (2025/26), £36.2m (2026/27), £46.5m (2027/28), £72.9m (2028/29), and £90.3m (2029/30). Government has a statutory override allowing the deficit to be carried on the balance sheet, but this expires 31 March 2028. Government announced on 9 February 2026 it will fund 90% of deficits as at 31 March 2026 subject to DfE approval of a SEND reform plan, but no details published on funding of deficits accrued during 2026/27 and 2027/28. Responsibility will transfer to central government from 2028, but significant uncertainty remains.
findings.matters: A £90.3m deficit on an area of statutory spending creates existential budget pressure. The expiry of the override forces the council to fund accumulated deficits from general resources unless government delivers on reform promises, creating off-balance-sheet risk that could materialise.
findings.quote: Forecasts over the medium term show an increasing deficit against DSG, this is detailed in Table K... As at 31 March 2025 the Council had a deficit on the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) reserve of £14.469m.

findings.headline: Medium-term cumulative funding gap grows from £44.937m in 2026/27 to £118.613m by 2030/31, with no credible plan to close it.
findings.detail: The Medium Term Financial Strategy identifies escalating funding gaps: £44.937m (2026/27), £58.964m (2027/28), £74.656m (2028/29), £94.107m (2029/30), and £118.613m (2030/31). The Section 25 statement notes failure to achieve planned savings will result in deficits rolling forward, and the Council must develop a Financial Recovery Plan setting out how it will reduce reliance on EFS and achieve sustainable budget position.
findings.matters: Structural deficits of this scale indicate the council cannot fund its current spending model. The growing gap suggests service cuts, further borrowing, or tax rises on an unsustainable trajectory.
findings.quote: The Board approved the Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) at its meeting on 11 September 2025. In summary, cumulative funding gaps of £44.937m in 2026/27, £58.964m in 2027/28, £74.656m in 2028/29, £94.107m in 2029/30, and £118.613m in 2030/31 were identified.

findings.headline: Council requires £33.873m Exceptional Financial Support in 2026/27 to balance budget, with total EFS borrowing reaching approximately £80m.
findings.detail: The council cannot balance its 2026/27 budget from council tax and business rates income. After receiving £224.237m in funding need against £190.364m in available funding (council tax and business rates), the £33.873m gap must be funded through capitalisation of revenue costs and 20-year PWLB borrowing. This brings forecast total EFS borrowing to approximately £80m. Government provisionally approved £35m EFS on 23 February 2026.
findings.matters: A council dependent on emergency borrowing to fund day-to-day operations represents material credit risk. The £80m total debt servicing cost and reliance on year-by-year government approval creates structural vulnerability.
findings.figures: £33.873m 2026/27 requirement; ~£80m total EFS borrowing over 20 years; £224.237m budget against £190.364m available funding
findings.quote: Table B forecasts the Council will have to borrow £33.873m in 2026/27 to provide a balanced budget. Without a credible savings plan being implemented over the next year, the unfunded deficit will roll forward to 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 26-27 - Final - after settlement (10-02-26), 12/02/2026 Executive Board
findings.headline: Mersey Gateway Bridge debt has an unconventional repayment structure where MRP is deferred until toll income is received
findings.detail: The council will not charge any Minimum Revenue Provision on Mersey Gateway Bridge expenditure until toll income is received. When income is received, MRP payments will be matched with income received. This creates a contingent liability where the repayment obligation depends on achieving projected toll revenues.
findings.matters: A lender needs visibility on this contingency. If toll income underperforms projections, the council will face an unexpected MRP charge in the future. The deferred MRP structure means current finances do not reflect the full cost of this infrastructure commitment.
findings.figures: Mersey Gateway expenditure treated under deferred MRP policy; amount included in capital spending but repayment contingent on toll income
findings.quote: One exception to the above is expenditure that the Council has incurred on the construction of the Mersey Gateway Bridge. As this debt will be repaid from future toll income the Council will not charge any MRP on this expenditure until the income is received. When received, MRP payments will be matched with income received thus having little impact on the Council's revenue budget.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 26-27 - Final - after settlement (10-02-26), 12/02/2026 Executive Board
findings.headline: Finance costs are rising while investment returns are falling, reducing the council's ability to offset borrowing costs with investment income
findings.detail: Short-term investment returns are expected to decline from 4.7% in 2025/26 to 3.5% in 2026/27 and remain at that level. Meanwhile, borrowing costs from PWLB are forecast at 4.6-5.8% depending on maturity. This widening gap between declining investment returns and stable borrowing costs reduces the council's financial flexibility.
findings.matters: Falling investment returns combined with escalating finance costs mean the council cannot rely on investment income to offset rising debt service costs, increasing pressure on the revenue budget.
findings.figures: Investment returns forecast: 4.7% (2025/26) declining to 3.5% (2026/27-2028/29). PWLB rates: 4.6% (5-year) to 5.8% (25-year)
findings.quote: Short term investment returns (up to three months) are expected to fall from 4.7% in 2025/26, to 3.50% in 2026/27, remaining at this level during 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 26-27 - Final - after settlement (10-02-26), 12/02/2026 Executive Board
findings.headline: The council is executing a heavy borrowing programme, having borrowed £80m in the last twelve months with £145m more planned for 2026/27
findings.detail: The council borrowed £80m in short-term loans over the past year (£50m PWLB, £30m from local authorities) to fund capital spending and Exceptional Financial Support. The strategy states it will replace this borrowing during 2026/27 plus borrow an additional £65m. The council acknowledges it maintains an under-borrowed position but faces ongoing cash needs.
findings.matters: The scale and pace of borrowing, combined with the council's explicit statement that 'it would not be possible to postpone borrowing due to economic conditions', indicates the council has limited flexibility and is dependent on access to borrowing markets to meet commitments.
findings.figures: £80m borrowed in last 12 months (£50m PWLB + £30m from other LAs). Additional borrowing planned: £65m in 2026/27
findings.quote: Due to the cost of funding the capital programme, and funding Exceptional Financial Support, the Council has borrowed £80m in short term loans over the last twelve months, £50m from PWLB and £30m from other Local Authorities. We expect to replace this borrowing during 26/27, as well as borrowing an additional £65m.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 26-27 - Final - after settlement (10-02-26), 12/02/2026 Executive Board
findings.headline: Finance costs as a percentage of net revenue budget are projected to more than triple from 3.8% to 12.7% over four years
findings.detail: The ratio of financing costs (net interest plus MRP) to the council's net revenue budget rises sharply from 3.8% in 2024/25 to 12.7% in 2028/29. This reflects both growing debt levels and the MRP charge increasing as the Capital Financing Requirement grows. Finance costs will rise from £5.7m to £24.7m annually.
findings.matters: A doubling of finance cost as a percentage of revenue indicates growing leverage and a shrinking operational budget available for service delivery. This trajectory needs to be sustainable and demonstrates increasing financial pressure.
findings.quote: Ratio of finance costs to net revenue stream 3.8% 6.3% 7.2% 9.9% 12.7%

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 26-27 - Final - after settlement (10-02-26), 12/02/2026 Executive Board
findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support capital commitments are growing rapidly and driving the council's borrowing needs
findings.detail: The council's Exceptional Financial Support capital programme rises from £33.9m in 2026/27 to £74.7m in 2028/29, representing an escalating commitment that will require sustained borrowing. By 2028/29, this single category accounts for 91% of projected capital spending. This growth is the primary driver of rising debt and finance costs.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council can sustain this trajectory of Exceptional Financial Support spending and service the resulting debt without squeezing other services or reserves.
findings.figures: Exceptional Financial Support capital: £33.9m (2026/27), £56.5m (2027/28), £74.7m (2028/29)
findings.quote: Exceptional Financial Support 10,000 30,666 33,872 56,503 74,735

findings.paper_title: AGB24Sept25 Draft Audit Findings Report Halton BC 2024-45 to AG Board.pdf
findings.headline: No formal authorization process for journals; only detective control exists through cost centre monitoring by budget holders
findings.detail: Auditors noted that the council has no formal review or authorization process for journals prior to posting. The mitigating control is that each cost centre is monitored by the relevant budget holder who reviews transactions periodically. Auditors recommended implementing a preventative control (pre-posting authorization) in addition to the existing detective control. This issue was carried forward from the prior year recommendation that management did not agree to implement.
findings.matters: Weak journal controls increase the risk of unauthorized or erroneous transactions being recorded in the accounts; the audit team specifically flagged this as a significant risk requiring a preventative control to align with best practice.
findings.figures: All journals affected
findings.quote: We noted that there continues to be no formal review or authorisation process for journals. The mitigating control is that each cost centre is monitored by the relevant budget holder.

findings.paper_title: AGB24Sept25 Draft Audit Findings Report Halton BC 2024-45 to AG Board.pdf
findings.headline: Ofsted inspection of Children's services rated council 'inadequate', requiring narrative report updates
findings.detail: The council received an 'inadequate' rating from a recent Ofsted inspection of Children's services. This required management to update the Narrative Report to clearly set out findings and conclusions from the inspection. This rating indicates serious service delivery deficiencies in a major council function.
findings.matters: An 'inadequate' Ofsted rating creates reputational risk, indicates management/operational failures, and may require intervention, all of which affect the council's ability to deliver services and manage resources effectively, which a lender would view as governance weakness.
findings.figures: Recent Ofsted inspection rating: 'inadequate'
findings.quote: Management have updated the Narrative Report to more clearly set out the findings and conclusions from the May 2024 Ofsted inspection of Children's services

findings.paper_title: AGB24Sept25 Draft Audit Findings Report Halton BC 2024-45 to AG Board.pdf
findings.headline: PFI liability increased £50.8m on IFRS 16 transition due to indexation of unitary charges, creating significant balance sheet impact
findings.detail: Implementation of IFRS 16 (Leases) from 1 April 2024 required restatement of PFI liabilities to reflect indexation of unitary payments since the start of schemes. This resulted in a £50.8m increase in the opening PFI liability at 1 April 2024. The PFI liability now stands at £385.8m at 31 March 2025 (£345.4m prior year), representing a significant increase in the council's long-term obligations.
findings.matters: The £50.8m PFI liability increase materially increases the council's debt burden and long-term financial commitments; a lender would need to assess the sustainability of these obligations alongside other financial pressures and the exceptional financial support requirement.
findings.figures: PFI liability £385.8m at 31 March 2025; £50.8m increase from IFRS 16 transition; prior year £345.4m
findings.quote: From 1 April 2024, the liability has been remeasured in accordance with IFRS 16 Leases, to reflect the impact of indexation of unitary charges up to the 31 March 2024. This resulted in restatement of the liability of £50.8m.

findings.paper_title: AGB24Sept25 Draft Audit Findings Report Halton BC 2024-45 to AG Board.pdf
findings.headline: £1.22m of capital expenditure recorded in wrong financial year, identified as unadjusted misstatement remaining in accounts
findings.detail: Testing of payments made after year-end identified three capital expenditure transactions totalling £1.22m that were incurred before 31 March 2025 but recorded in 2025/26. This capital expenditure cut-off error was not adjusted in the final accounts and remains unadjusted. Auditors recommended management implement controls to review capital expenditure around year-end.
findings.matters: Material cut-off errors in capital expenditure recording suggest weak year-end controls and could indicate misstatement of both years' financial positions; a lender would be concerned about the reliability of financial reporting controls.
findings.figures: £1.22m capital expenditure incorrectly recorded in 2025/26; three transactions involved
findings.quote: Our substantive testing of payments made after the year-end to confirm the completeness of expenditure recorded in the financial year identified 3 errors totalling £1.22m whereby transactions were recorded in 2025/26 which related to 2024/25. These all related to capital expenditure incurred before 31 March 2025, but recorded in April and May 2025.

findings.paper_title: AGB24Sept25 Draft Audit Findings Report Halton BC 2024-45 to AG Board.pdf
findings.headline: £11.2m of fully depreciated assets incorrectly held on fixed asset register after disposal, indicating asset tracking and disposal control failures
findings.detail: Audit testing identified that £11.2m of fully depreciated assets were incorrectly held on the Fixed Asset Register despite being disposed of or no longer in use. Initial sample testing found all 5 items selected were incorrectly held, leading to a full review that identified this material population. This was adjusted in the accounts but indicates systematic failures in asset disposal tracking.
findings.matters: Material errors in asset tracking suggest weak internal controls over a significant balance sheet area; auditors have recommended management implement procedures to regularly review assets nearing end of life and identify unrecorded disposals.
findings.figures: £11.2m of assets identified as disposed but incorrectly held; total fully depreciated assets on register £18.3m
findings.quote: At 31 March 2025, there were fully depreciated assets with a total gross cost of £18.3m on the Fixed Asset Register. Our substantive testing of fully depreciated assets identified that all 5 items selected in our initial sample and one further item were subsequently confirmed to have been disposed of and were incorrectly held on the Fixed Asset Register.

findings.paper_title: AGB24Sept25 Draft Audit Findings Report Halton BC 2024-45 to AG Board.pdf
findings.headline: £5.8m understatement of land and buildings asset value due to use of incorrect valuation report, adjusted in final accounts
findings.detail: The auditors identified that the draft accounts and fixed asset register had been updated based on an incorrect version of the valuation report from the council's external valuer (Sanderson Weatherall), resulting in a £5.8m understatement of Land & Buildings. The adjustment was made in the final accounts. This highlights weaknesses in reconciliation and quality review procedures between external valuers and account preparation.
findings.matters: A £5.8m error in asset valuation suggests weak internal controls over financial data from external experts and raises concerns about the reliability of the council's financial position; lenders rely on accurate asset valuations for security assessment.
findings.figures: £5.8m understatement; Land & Buildings valued at £229m at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: Our review of identified that the draft accounts did not reconcile to the final valuation report issued by Sanderson Weatherall. This has resulted in an understatement of Land & Buildings of £5.8m, which has been adjusted in the accounts

findings.paper_title: AGB24Sept25 Draft Audit Findings Report Halton BC 2024-45 to AG Board.pdf
findings.headline: Council required emergency capitalisation direction from government, with only partial approval after requesting £20.8m for 2024/25
findings.detail: In December 2024, the council requested Exceptional Financial Support from MHCLG for £20.8m in 2024/25 and £32m in 2025/26. After external assurance review, the council obtained final approval for a capitalisation direction of only £10m for 2024/25, meaning £10.8m of the originally-requested revenue support was not approved. This indicates the council cannot fund operations through normal means.
findings.matters: Exceptional Financial Support requirement demonstrates the council cannot fund its operations from revenue and requires government emergency intervention; lenders would view this as indicating severe financial distress and raising questions about normal borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £20.8m requested for 2024/25; £32m requested for 2025/26; £10m approved capitalisation direction for 2024/25
findings.quote: In December 2024 the Council requested Exceptional Financial Support from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) in respect of the financial years 2024/25 and 2025/26. At the time of audit planning, the Council have received approval that the Deputy Prime Minister (DPM) is minded to approve a capitalisation direction of £20.8 million in 2024/25 and £32 million in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: AGB24Sept25 Draft Audit Findings Report Halton BC 2024-45 to AG Board.pdf
findings.headline: Auditors identified significant weaknesses in council's financial sustainability arrangements and are issuing additional statutory recommendations
findings.detail: The auditors are not satisfied that the council has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness. In November 2024, they issued two statutory recommendations under section 24 schedule 7 of the Local Audit and Accountability Act 2014 relating to financial sustainability and current financial challenges. They are minded to issue additional recommendations for 2024/25. The auditors completed their VFM work and identified significant weaknesses in the council's arrangements.
findings.matters: Statutory recommendations signal that auditors believe the council faces serious financial governance problems requiring intervention; a lender would view this as a significant red flag for repayment capacity and management capability.
findings.figures: Two statutory recommendations issued November 2024; additional recommendations being prepared for 2024/25
findings.quote: We identified significant weaknesses in the Council's arrangements and so are not satisfied that the Council has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources.

findings.headline: No Financial Recovery Plan outcomes or timescales disclosed in this document; savings target is unquantified.
findings.detail: The MTFS notes that a Financial Recovery Plan is presented as a separate agenda item and sets out "the scale of the savings required to return the Council to a sustainable budget position over the medium-term." This MTFS does not quantify the savings target or detail the recovery strategy. The council states the scale of savings needed "will be extremely difficult to implement" but provides no breakdown or probability assessment.
findings.matters: Without a named savings plan and deliverability evidence, the council's route out of deficit is unclear. A lender needs to know if management has a credible recovery strategy.
findings.figures: Total savings required estimated at £118.6m cumulative; annual savings rising from £15.6m (2026/27) to £24.5m (2030/31)
findings.quote: The forecast shows that it is vital that a significant level of budget savings are achieved over the next five years, the scale of which will be extremely difficult to implement.

findings.headline: Section 114 risk: if EFS is not approved, the finance officer must issue a notice; government may then take control.
findings.detail: If MHCLG refuses an EFS application, the Section 151 Officer must issue a Section 114 notice, triggering an immediate council meeting and a 21-day action plan to balance the budget. Government may then appoint commissioners to run the council directly or issue direct instructions. The document warns the council must "adopt a Section 114 attitude" to all spending and urgently agree a recovery plan.
findings.matters: Section 114 is a public acknowledgement of insolvency and loss of democratic control. It signals to lenders that the council cannot manage its finances independently.
findings.figures: Section 114 requires budget balance within 21 days; government may intervene directly or appoint commissioners
findings.quote: If MHCLG do not approve an application for EFS, the Section 151 Officer of any council which cannot set a balanced budget, will be required to issue a Section 114 Notice under the Local Government Finance Act 1988. Once the Notice is issued, no new spending can be undertaken without authorisation of the Section 151 Officer, and the council must meet within 21 days to discuss how to reduce expenditure to match the funding available.

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review is the first major funding system reform since 2013/14; estimated benefit £10.45m but heavily uncertain.
findings.detail: A new funding formula will determine each council's needs-based allocation. Halton expects to gain ~£10.45m over three years (phased in 2026/27–2028/29). However, the government has not published the data underlying the formula, and key details (business rates reset scope, grant roll-ins, transitional protections) remain undefined. The council's estimate is contingent on multiple assumptions, any of which could change.
findings.matters: The council is betting the forecast on a £10.45m gain from a reform that is not yet finalised. If the benefit is smaller, or delayed, the deficit widens significantly.
findings.figures: ~£10.45m estimated increase in Core Spending Power over three years; phased 2026/27–2028/29
findings.quote: It is anticipated that Halton's Core Spending Power will increase as a result of the Fair Funding Review. The current best estimate of the impact of the Fair Funding Review is that Core Spending Power is expected to increase by approximately £10.45m, assuming that all Business Rates growth is lost, with this increase phased-in over three years from 2026/27 to 2028/29.

findings.headline: Business rates pilot scheme ends 2026/27, withdrawing retained growth income to government.
findings.detail: Halton is part of the Liverpool City Region 100% business rates retention pilot. This allows the council to keep all growth above the baseline. The scheme ends 31 March 2026. From 2026/27, all growth will be returned to government for redistribution. The MTFS assumes loss of this income; the council has written to MHCLG seeking clarity on whether any accumulated growth can be retained, but received no answer.
findings.matters: Loss of business rates growth removes a key income source with no announced replacement. The Fair Funding Review may compensate, but the document notes high uncertainty.
findings.figures: 100% business rates pilot ends 2026/27; £1.5bn in growth nationally is being retained and will be redistributed
findings.quote: There has been no information published by Government on whether the 100% business rates pilots will continue to operate beyond 2025/26, and if so, whether any of the growth accumulated within the schemes can be retained. For the purposes of this forecast, it has been assumed that the pilot scheme will cease to operate in 2026/27, and that all growth will returned to Government for redistribution within the Settlement.

findings.headline: General reserves depleted to £5.1m (2.81% of net budget), insufficient to absorb any overspend.
findings.detail: The council explicitly states its general reserve is insufficient and no longer available to balance future budgets. At £5.149m, it represents only 2.81% of the 2025/26 net budget. All other reserves (£55.151m) are earmarked for specific purposes. This leaves zero discretion to manage shocks or misjudgements.
findings.matters: A council with minimal unallocated reserves cannot absorb forecast errors or service pressures. Any adverse variance in demand or funding will require immediate government intervention.
findings.figures: General reserve £5.149m (2.81% of net budget); earmarked reserves £55.151m (all committed); total liquid reserves insufficient
findings.quote: As at 31 July 2025 the balance of the Council's general reserve was £5.149m. The general reserve balance represents 2.81% of the Council's 2025/26 net budget. This level of General Reserve is considered to be insufficient and provides little to cover unforeseen costs.

findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support is conditional on an external assurance review; no date yet set.
findings.detail: The £29.385m EFS approval for 2025/26 is pending completion of an external assurance review by MHCLG. The review will assess the council's financial position and governance arrangements. The council has not been given a date for this assessment. Until it completes, there is no certainty of funding for 2025/26, and any criticism could jeopardise future EFS applications.
findings.matters: A lender cannot assume EFS will continue if government loses confidence. The undated review is a sword of Damocles; a critical report could force immediate Section 114 action.
findings.figures: £29.385m EFS for 2025/26 approval conditional on review
findings.quote: EFS approval for 2025/26 is pending the Council undergoing an external assurance review which will include, but will not be limited to, an assessment of the council's financial position and governance arrangements. No date has yet been fixed for the assessment

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit will reach £77.6m by 2030/31; statutory protections end March 2028.
findings.detail: Halton holds a DSG deficit of £23.5m (2025/26) forecast to grow to £77.6m (2029/30). Currently, a government statutory override prevents this hitting the general fund. That override expires 31 March 2028. Unless extended or replaced, the council will be forced to fund £77.6m from general fund resources—equivalent to 54% of the council's 2030/31 annual spending—in a single year.
findings.matters: The override is a temporary reprieve. Once it expires, the council must either secure a deficit waiver or fund the entire shortfall from revenue, making insolvency certain unless the deficit is resolved first.
findings.quote: Without further government intervention, DSG deficits will need to be funded from General Fund resources from 1st April 2028.

findings.headline: Social care spending is significantly higher than comparator councils and is rising faster than forecast inflation.
findings.detail: Halton spends more per head on both adult and children's social care than peer councils. The MTFS assumes 4% annual cost inflation on social care contracts (vs. 2% general), driven by the National Living Wage. Demand growth assumptions of 11.1% (adult) and 4.5% (children) are built into the forecast, but the council's current per-head spend already exceeds comparators, suggesting demand management may be failing.
findings.matters: High social care spending is a structural problem, not a cyclical one. It will not improve without either demand reduction (placements, hours) or service redesign, neither of which is promised in this document.
findings.figures: £5.595m adult demand pressure (2026/27), rising to £8.531m (2030/31); £1.473m children's demand (2026/27), rising to £1.758m (2030/31)
findings.quote: The Council spend against social care areas is significantly higher on a per head basis than comparator authorities and urgent action is required over the MTFS period to bring this down.

findings.headline: Current in-year spending is £5.6m over budget (31 July 2025) with no corrective plan named.
findings.detail: Seven weeks into 2025/26, the council is already £1.629m overspent. If trends continue, year-end overspend reaches £5.572m. The document names the drivers—children's social care, adult social care, and home-to-school transport—but does not detail the corrective actions or their likelihood of success.
findings.matters: In-year overspends signal either forecasting failure or demand exceeding budget. Either way, it foreshadows larger deficits ahead unless spending control tightens immediately.
findings.figures: £1.629m overspent at 31 July 2025; £5.572m forecast outturn overspend if no action taken
findings.quote: As at 31 July 2025 the net Council spending position is £1.629m over budget. The outturn forecast for the year estimates that net spending will be over budget by £5.572m if no corrective action is taken.

findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support costs forecast to reach £32.9m annually by 2030/31, with £39.4m already drawn.
findings.detail: The council has borrowed £10m (2024/25) and £29.385m (2025/26) via Exceptional Financial Support—a government capitalisation scheme that funds current revenue deficits through 20-year PWLB borrowing. At current borrowing costs (£1m per £10m borrowed), annual debt service will reach £32.935m by 2030/31, consuming 15% of total resources. This is not sustainable funding; it merely defers the problem.
findings.matters: EFS is temporary; every £1 borrowed costs the revenue budget ~£0.1/year for 20 years. A lender needs to know if the council can service this debt once EFS runs out or reforms.
findings.figures: £10m (2024/25) + £29.385m (2025/26) already taken; forecast £3.327m–£10.023m annual costs 2026/27–2030/31; reaching £32.935m by 2030/31 (15% of resources)
findings.quote: Each £10m of borrowing taken will increase revenue costs by approximately £1m. £10m of EFS was used to finance spending in the 2024/25 financial year, and £29.385m was used in setting the 2025/26 budget.

findings.headline: A £118.6m cumulative funding gap by 2030/31, representing 54% of estimated resources.
findings.detail: The council projects spending will exceed available funding by £118.613m over five years if current spending levels are maintained. This is explicitly described as a structural budget deficit with no savings plan yet proven to close the gap. The in-year deficits range from £15.6m (2026/27) to £24.5m (2030/31) even after assumed council tax increases.
findings.matters: A deficit of this scale means the council cannot deliver a balanced budget through normal budget management; it signals insolvency risk without radical service cuts or government intervention.
findings.figures: £118.613m cumulative gap; 54% of 2030/31 resources; in-year gaps of £15,552k–£24,506k
findings.quote: the gap between the Council's expenditure and the resources available is estimated to be £118.613m by 2030/31 if current levels of spending are maintained. This represents 54% of the Council's estimated resources in 2030/31.

news_drafts.headline: PWLB rates rose sharply in March 2026 as gilt market sold off on geopolitical risk
news_drafts.lead: Rate environment directly impacts refinance costs; £50m position coming due in 2026/27 will face these elevated rates

news_drafts.headline: Short-term borrowing from 2024/25 must be refinanced in 2026/27 at substantially higher rates
news_drafts.lead: Rising refinance costs reduce budget flexibility and increase vulnerability to further rate movements; overspending-driven borrowing is a structural concern, not temporary

news_drafts.headline: PFI restatement increased liabilities by £50.8m and breached operational borrowing limits
news_drafts.lead: Operational boundary breaches signal forecasting or governance failure, and PFI liabilities constrain a council's future borrowing capacity and cash flexibility
